about: How the edge of a country is marked where an old road leaves it: by what the kingdom after the makers set at its bounds (by its kind: warlords, abbots, princes), and by the lie of the land (by terrain). A country's borders are drawn from both, each border its own, so that no two read alike. {region} is the country's name, {kingdom} the kingdom's; the sign of the country beyond is said after. Written by hand.

warlords: The road passes a ruined watch-post on a knoll: four walls of a tower with no roof, an arrow-slit in each, and the stump of a beacon-post where the lords of {kingdom} watched their bounds.
Where the road leaves {region} it goes through a gap in an old bank and ditch, thrown up across the way by the lords of {kingdom}; the gate that hung in it is gone, but its posts stand.
abbots: A wayside cross of the brothers of {kingdom} stands where the road leaves {region}, a cross cut in a pillar of old stone with the makers' marks still under it, and a dish at its foot for offerings.
At the edge of {region} the road goes past a hermit's cell built against a rock: one room, its door open, a bed of stone, and the brothers' sign cut over the lintel.
princes: Where the road leaves {region} there is a toll-house with its windows out and a bar across the road, rotted through, that the merchant-princes of {kingdom} once let down at dusk.
A milestone stands by the road at the edge of {region}, cut with the merchant-princes' ship and the distances to places whose names have worn away.

marsh: The road comes to the edge of {region} on a causeway of logs, and a tall post stands in the water beside it with a fish-basket hung on it and a mark cut at the top, where the bounds were set.
At the edge of {region} a beacon stands on stilts above the reeds, a fire-basket rusted open at the top, so that the bounds could be found in fog.
forest: At the edge of {region} the road goes between two great oaks blazed with the same sign, so old that the bark has grown over half of it.
Where the road leaves {region} a wooden post carved with faces stands in a clearing, grey as stone, the faces on the far side different from these.
mountain: The road reaches the edge of {region} at a cairn on the top of a pass, every stone in it carried up by someone going over; you add one, as everyone does.
At the edge of {region} the road goes through a notch in the ridge, and a line of stones set on end crosses the notch from side to side.
frost: At the edge of {region} a ring of stones stands half-buried in old snow beside the road, with one stone taller than the rest, its face toward this side.
Where the road leaves {region} there is a pole with a horse's skull on it, put up to say whose land this is, and a newer skull beside it.
plain: A march-stone as tall as a man stands by the road where it leaves {region}. On this side it is cut with the sign of {region}; on the far side, with a sign you do not know.
desert: Where the road leaves {region} a cairn of white stones stands on a low rise, a water-skin hung empty on a stake beside it, so that whoever comes in knows how far the next well is.
At the edge of {region} the road passes between two posts of sun-bleached timber, and on one of them someone has cut the number of days to the next water.
